lessons.title: What Is Prompting?
lessons.subtitle: Programming in prose

blocks.text: A prompt is the input you give a language model. Prompt engineering is the practice of writing that input so the model reliably produces what you actually need - not just something reasonable-looking.

It matters because the model has no access to your intent. It sees text and continues it. Everything it needs to know - the goal, the audience, the format, the constraints - has to be present in what you wrote.

rows: A 200-word article for children about caring for a puppy
Find the bug causing the crash and explain the fix
Three bullet points a busy manager can read in 15 seconds

blocks.title: Specificity beats cleverness
blocks.body: There are no magic words. The prompts that work are the ones that state the task, the audience, the format and the constraints plainly. Most 'prompt hacks' are just specificity in disguise.

summaryPoints: The model only knows what the prompt tells it
Vague prompts produce generically plausible, rarely useful output
Specificity about task, audience, format and constraints is the whole skill

lessons.title: The Anatomy of a Good Prompt
lessons.subtitle: Five components, in order

blocks.text: Effective prompts tend to share a structure. You will not need every component every time, but knowing them turns prompting from guesswork into a checklist.

blocks.title: Prompt components
nodes: Role - who the model is acting as
Format - the exact shape of the answer
blocks.caption: Instruction is mandatory; the rest earn their place as needed.
The same request, unstructured and structured.
blocks.code:
WEAK:
Summarise this customer feedback.

STRONG:
You are a product analyst reviewing customer feedback.

Context: These are support tickets from the last 30 days for our
mobile banking app. The team wants to decide what to fix next quarter.

Task: Identify the three most frequently reported problems.

Constraints:
- Base every claim only on the tickets provided
- If a theme appears fewer than 3 times, exclude it
- Do not propose solutions - identification only

Format: For each problem give a one-line title, the number of
mentions, and one representative verbatim quote.

Tickets:
<<<
{tickets}
>>>

blocks.title: Use delimiters for injected data
blocks.body: The triple angle brackets above matter. They mark where your data starts and stops, so the model does not mistake content inside a ticket for an instruction to follow. Any clear delimiter works - XML-style tags, triple backticks - as long as it is used consistently.

blocks.title: Say what to do, not what to avoid
blocks.body: 'Do not be verbose' is weaker than 'Answer in at most three sentences'. Negative instructions require the model to infer the acceptable region; positive instructions describe it directly.

summaryPoints: Role, context, instruction, constraints and format are the reusable components
Delimiters separate your data from your instructions
Positive instructions outperform prohibitions

lessons.title: Role Prompting and Context
lessons.subtitle: Setting the frame

blocks.text: Assigning a role - 'You are an experienced paediatric nurse' - shifts vocabulary, depth and assumed audience. It is a compact way to communicate a great deal about the register you want.

blocks.title: A role is not expertise
blocks.body: Telling a model it is a doctor does not give it medical knowledge it lacks, and it does not make its answers safe to act on. Role prompting changes style and framing. It does not change what the model knows or how reliable it is.

blocks.text: Context is usually the bigger lever

Roles are widely discussed; context does more work. Supplying the actual background - who the audience is, what has already been tried, what constraints exist - improves output far more than any persona.

rows: Readers are first-year students with no programming background
This will go in a board pack, not a technical document
We already tried caching; it did not help
Must work on Android 7 and above
A reader should be able to act on this without asking follow-ups

summaryPoints: Role prompting adjusts tone, vocabulary and assumed audience
It does not add knowledge or make output trustworthy
Concrete context about audience, purpose and constraints matters more

lessons.title: Zero-Shot and Few-Shot Prompting
lessons.subtitle: Teaching by example

rows: Common tasks the model already handles well
When the output format needs demonstrating
Unusual formats, subtle distinctions, consistent labelling

blocks.text: Few-shot prompting works because examples communicate things that are tedious to describe. Showing three correctly formatted outputs conveys the spacing, the tone and the level of detail more precisely than a paragraph of specification.

blocks.caption: Few-shot for a nuanced classification.
blocks.code:
Classify each support message by urgency.

Message: "App crashes every time I open it"
Urgency: HIGH
Reason: Complete loss of function

Message: "Would be nice to have dark mode"
Urgency: LOW
Reason: Feature request, no impairment

Message: "Payment went through twice"
Urgency: HIGH
Reason: Financial impact requiring reversal

Message: "The font on the settings page looks slightly off"
Urgency: LOW
Reason: Cosmetic, no functional impact

Message: "Cannot log in since this morning's update"
Urgency:

blocks.title: Cover the edges, not the obvious
blocks.body: The most valuable examples are the ambiguous ones. Two examples covering the boundary between HIGH and LOW teach far more than five obvious cases. If a distinction is subtle, demonstrate it explicitly.

blocks.title: Examples carry bias
blocks.body: If every example you provide happens to be HIGH urgency, the model will over-predict HIGH. Balance your examples across the classes you expect, or you will bake a skew into every output.

summaryPoints: Zero-shot uses instructions alone; few-shot adds demonstrations
Examples convey format and nuance more precisely than description
Cover ambiguous boundary cases, and keep examples balanced across classes

lessons.title: Structured Outputs
lessons.subtitle: Making output that software can consume

blocks.text: When a model's output feeds another program rather than a person, free-form prose is a liability. You need a predictable structure that parses every time.

blocks.caption: Specify the schema explicitly.
blocks.code:
Extract the details of this event.

Return ONLY valid JSON matching this schema, with no surrounding
text, explanation or markdown fences:

{
  "title": string,
  "date": string (ISO 8601, YYYY-MM-DD),
  "location": string | null,
  "attendee_count": integer | null,
  "confidence": "high" | "medium" | "low"
}

If a field is not stated in the text, use null. Do not guess.

Text:
<<<
{input_text}
>>>

items: State the schema, including types and which fields may be null
Say 'return only JSON' - models otherwise wrap it in prose or code fences
Give an explicit rule for missing data, or the model will invent values
Use the API's native structured-output or tool-calling mode when available - it enforces the schema rather than requesting it

blocks.title: Always parse defensively
blocks.body: Even with a perfect prompt, wrap parsing in error handling. Strip stray code fences, and have a fallback for a malformed response. A pipeline that crashes on one bad parse is a pipeline that will page you at 3am.

summaryPoints: Specify the exact schema, types and null-handling rules
Native structured-output modes enforce the schema rather than asking for it
Parse defensively regardless - responses will occasionally be malformed

lessons.title: Prompt Chaining
lessons.subtitle: Breaking one hard task into several easy ones

blocks.text: A prompt asking for six things at once usually does all six mediocrely. Chaining splits the work into steps, feeding each output into the next prompt.

blocks.title: A review-analysis chain
nodes: Step 3: Rank themes by frequency and severity
Step 4: Draft recommendations for the top three
blocks.caption: Each step is simple enough to verify before the next runs.

items: Each step has one clear objective, so instructions stay unambiguous
Intermediate output is inspectable, so you can see exactly where quality broke
Steps can use different settings - extraction at temperature 0, drafting warmer
Individual steps can be retried without redoing the whole pipeline

blocks.title: Errors compound
blocks.body: The trade-off is that a mistake in step 1 propagates through everything downstream. Validate between steps - a schema check or a sanity assertion - rather than assuming each stage succeeded.

summaryPoints: Chaining splits a complex task into single-purpose steps
Intermediate results are inspectable and independently retryable
Validate between steps, because early errors propagate

lessons.title: Reasoning-Oriented Prompting
lessons.subtitle: Asking for the working, not just the answer

blocks.text: For multi-step problems, asking a model to work through its reasoning before answering measurably improves accuracy. The generated reasoning becomes part of the context the final answer is conditioned on.

blocks.caption: Chain-of-thought prompting.
blocks.code:
A shop sells notebooks at 3 for 12 currency units. Priya buys 7
notebooks and pays with a 50 note. How much change does she get?

Work through this step by step, showing each calculation, then
give the final answer on its own line prefixed with 'Answer:'.

blocks.title: Why it helps
blocks.body: A model produces one token at a time with a fixed amount of computation per token. Forcing intermediate steps gives it more computation to spend on the problem, and lets each step build on a written record of the last, rather than holding everything implicitly.

items: Self-consistency - sample several independent reasoning paths and take the majority answer
Least-to-most - solve the simplest sub-problem first, then build up
Step-back prompting - ask for the general principle before the specific case

blocks.title: Reasoning models change the calculus
blocks.body: Newer reasoning models perform this internally and are often instructed not to be given explicit chain-of-thought prompts, which can interfere. Check the guidance for the model you are using rather than applying the technique reflexively.

blocks.title: Stated reasoning is not actual reasoning
blocks.body: The written steps are a plausible-looking explanation, not a transcript of the model's internal process. A model can produce flawless-looking reasoning and a wrong answer, or correct answers via nonsense steps. Verify conclusions, not just whether the working looks tidy.

summaryPoints: Requesting step-by-step working improves multi-step accuracy
It gives the model more computation and an explicit record to build on
Written reasoning is a plausible explanation, not a faithful internal trace

lessons.title: Debugging and Optimising Prompts
lessons.subtitle: A systematic method, not trial and error

blocks.text: Most people debug prompts by rewriting them at random until something works. That produces a prompt you cannot reason about and cannot safely change. A method works better.

items: Build a small test set - 10 to 20 representative inputs with known good outputs
Establish a baseline by running your current prompt against all of them
Change exactly one thing, then re-run the whole set
Keep the change only if the score improves; revert it otherwise
Re-test the full set after every change, not just the case you were fixing

blocks.title: Fixing one case often breaks another
blocks.body: This is the reason to keep a test set. Adding an instruction to solve one failure regularly degrades three cases that previously worked - and without re-running everything, you will not notice until production does.

rows: State an explicit limit in words or sentences
Add a worked example of the exact output
Buried in the middle of a long prompt
Move critical instructions to the start or end
No grounding, and no permission to decline
Supply source text; allow 'not stated in the source'
State the legitimate purpose and context plainly
Set temperature to 0 for deterministic tasks

blocks.title: Version your prompts
blocks.body: Production prompts are code. Keep them in source control with their test cases, so you can see what changed, review it, and roll back a regression the same way you would any other deployment.

summaryPoints: Debug against a fixed test set, changing one variable at a time
Always re-run every case - local fixes cause regressions elsewhere
Treat production prompts as versioned, reviewable code
